title: A finite arithmetic test for simplicity of the Riemann zeros, after Suzuki
subject: math.NT
abstract: M. Suzuki proved that, under the Riemann hypothesis, the compressions of the inverse of a self-adjoint differentiation operator to windows of Weil's quadratic form converge in Hilbert-Schmidt norm, and that their eigenvalues recover every distinct zero ordinate of the Riemann zeta function; he notes that the multiplicities are not recovered. The Riemann hypothesis is now a theorem of L. Alpöge. We show that the multiplicities are recovered by even trace powers. Let $S_k=2\sum_{\gamma>0}m_\gamma\gamma^{-2k}$ be the Taylor moments of $\log\xi(1/2+iz)$, which count multiplicity, and let $D_{N,k}$ be $S_k$ minus the trace of the $2k$-th power of a finite compression whose matrix entries come from the explicit formula with finitely many prime powers. Then $D_{N,k}\ge 2E(T)/T^{2k}$, where $E(T)$ is the number of repeated zeros up to height $T$ counted with their excess multiplicity, and $\sup_{N,k}(2/D_{N,k})^{1/(2k)}$ equals the height of the first multiple zero. So the zeros up to a height $T$ are simple if and only if one finite arithmetic inequality holds, and all zeros are simple if and only if these heights are unbounded. An equivalent integer form counts the positive eigenvalues of one Hermitian matrix. A computation in ball arithmetic, with prime powers below $e^{12}$ and no zero ordinates as input, certifies that every zero with $0<\Im\rho\le 97.632$ is simple. The mathematics was produced by GPT-6 Astra (ChatGPT Pro mode); Claude Opus 5.5 at effort high checked every proof, wrote this text, and recomputed the certificate with an independently written program. No human has checked this note.
comments: This note answers, under Alpöge's theorem, the remark of M. Suzuki (arXiv:2610.32704, Section 1) that his compressions of Weil's quadratic form do not recover the multiplicities of the zeta zeros; the Hilbert space, the operator and the convergence of compressions are Suzuki's. The principle that a finite restriction of Weil's form sees distinct zeros through its rank or positive index and counted zeros through its trace is Alpöge and Furman's (arXiv:2608.13637v2, Prop. 4.1, p. 6), as is the pull-back of inertia used in Theorem 2 (Lemma 3.1, p. 5); their results, like Lamzouri's (arXiv:2609.02882) and Mori's window bounds (Zenodo 24281606), give proportions, while this note gives an exact test at each height. On Hexagon, P. Caceres (hexagon:2610.00688, Part IV) gives an averaged criterion involving simple zeros.
